title: Who Is Allowed To Merge
eyebrow: Landed, after sixteen readings that found seventy-seven more faults. Every one is now fixed and held down by a check that goes red without it; your three own projects are untouched.

content.label: What changed for the shared work project
content.lead: Every route found open is now shut. Each row was put to the guard as it is actually installed, in the real company checkout, not to the change on its own.

rows: Fold a piece of work into staging or main
Send either line up to the company copy
Bring work in by pulling instead of folding
Accept a waiting piece of work from the command line
Accept it through the code-hosting site's raw interface — in any of its three forms — instead
Drag another line straight onto staging without folding at all
Write a change straight onto the line it is standing on
Point one of those lines at its own work, or rename it away
Step onto staging and fold in, as one single command
Do any of the above from inside another project's copy

blocks.label: And in every way of typing it, which is where the work went
blocks.text: The same push is refused with the line in quotes, with a plus in front, spelled as the position it is standing at, behind env or sudo or timeout — with or without those words' own switches — handed to a second shell, aimed by a directory switch or a setting, written with the tool's full path, or on the second line of the call. Sixteen readings by someone who did not write it found seventy-seven of these, one at a time.

content.label: What an agent can still do there
content.lead: The whole normal working day, unchanged. Seven for seven, run from the shared work project while it stands on staging.

items: Start a line of its own, in either spelling, and commit onto it.

Bring staging into its own work, and rebase its own work onto staging — including all the conflict resolution that comes with either. Your explicit condition, and it is what a guard reading only the word would have blocked.
Stage, stash, and look at what changed against staging.
Open the work up for your review.

blocks.label: So the only thing taken away
blocks.text: Writing to what the team ships. Everything an agent does to prepare work, and every way it stays current with what other people have shipped, is exactly as it was.

content.label: What the readings cost, and what they were worth
content.lead: The change was read sixteen times by someone who did not write it. Every reading sent it back.

rows: A line named in quotes was read as no line at all, so every refusal was one keystroke away
A project joining with a board and no answer could never finish a piece of work
Bringing work in by pulling — the spelling the session briefing itself tells an agent to use
Any word in front of the command walked past the guard untouched
Reaching into another project's copy was judged by the rules of the copy you started in
Handing the command to a second shell opened every route again
Bringing your own line up to date was being refused — the guard blocking correct work
Dragging a line onto staging without folding, and the site's raw merge call, were both unwatched
Naming the line through a plain variable walked past everything — one dollar sign
Somebody else's code checked out inside one of your projects was borrowing your project's permission
A commit whose message happened to read like a mid-job switch stood its own command down
A command written inside an if or a loop was not read as a command by either guard
From one of your own projects, an agent could still merge a waiting piece of work in the company's
The code-hosting site has two more ways onto a shipping line, and neither was watched
A line name fed in from a pipe, and a setting exported on its own line, both walked past everything
A second shell fed its commands rather than given them, which reopened every route at once

blocks.label: Nothing was taken on trust
blocks.text: Eighty-three deliberate breakages are put back one at a time and each one has to turn a check red. The run fails rather than reporting a fault nothing noticed, and it stops rather than reporting success if the code it breaks has moved.

blocks.label: Four of the faults were in your own projects, not the shared one
blocks.text: Staying current was being treated as landing; every ordinary commit briefly queued behind the token meant for folds; a command quoted inside a written note was read as a command being run — found when the guard refused one of this job's own notes; and the racing project's own compile gate had started failing your pushes whenever the shared tools moved underneath it, which is now a warning that costs a third of a second.

content.label: What it cost you
content.lead: One line each in three files you own, and nothing anywhere else.

rows: That an agent lands its own work here. Written once each, in the file where each project already describes itself
Nothing at all. It is protected because it has never said otherwise, which is the answer you picked
Somebody else's code checked out inside your project
Also nothing, and it is now protected in its own right rather than borrowing yours — the vendored dependency in your racing project was open until this round
A team project that later runs a board
One line naming which lines are off limits. It is told exactly that, in the refusal itself, rather than quietly never finishing a job

decisions.title: The guard stops asking whether your board is running
decisions.why: It is switched off in exactly the project that needs it most. Protecting a line other people ship from has nothing to do with whether work is being tracked on a board, and tying the two together is what left the gap.

decisions.title: Every way in is covered, not just the obvious one
decisions.why: Today's guard watches only one of the four routes onto a line. Closing one and leaving three open reads as protection and is not, which is worse than no guard at all — you would stop checking.

decisions.title: A protected project that runs a board names a line its agents may land on
decisions.why: Forbidding the fold outright jams the board permanently, because a piece of work only counts as done once it reaches what the project ships. So a project is taken at its word about which lines are off limits, leaving one its agents can finish on, and a project that has joined without answering is told exactly that in the refusal rather than quietly never finishing anything.

decisions.title: The policy is stated by each project, never by naming projects inside the shared tools
decisions.why: A shared tool that knows the name of one project has stopped being shared. Every difference between your projects is already declared this way.

decisions.title: Written instructions are not counted as protection
decisions.why: The shared work project already asks an agent to check before offering work up. It is a good instruction and it holds most of the time; the point of a guard is the day it does not.

decisions.title: What a command writes to is the only question asked
decisions.why: Your two conditions — conflicts resolved while folding, and a line brought up to date from another — are not exceptions to the rule under this reading, they fall out of it. A guard that matched on the word instead would need a list of exceptions, and a list of exceptions is where the next hole comes from.

decisions.title: The one-at-a-time token still only queues folds, not every write
decisions.why: Reading what a command writes to briefly made it queue ordinary commits as well, which stopped every session committing in its own copy. It is scoped back to folds and held there by a case that goes red if it ever widens again.

decisions.title: Nothing was run against the company copy to prove any of this
decisions.why: Every route was put to the guard the way the harness puts it, and the ones needing a real project were run against a scratch one built for the purpose. Proving a guard by tripping it on somebody's live work is not proof worth having.

decisions.title: A name only the running shell can settle is refused for being unreadable, not for being every line
decisions.why: Sending up the line you are standing on is often typed by asking git which line that is, and nothing can read the answer before the command runs. Refusing it as though it wrote to everything, and offering the project-wide opt-out as the way out, teaches an agent to switch the guard off over an ordinary command. It is now told what it cannot be read as and the one-word spelling that works.

decisions.title: Every fix ships with a deliberate breakage that proves the check would catch it
decisions.why: A check that passes proves the code passes it, not that it would notice the fault coming back. Eighty-three breakages are put back one at a time; the run fails if any of them leaves everything green, and stops rather than reporting success if the code it breaks has moved.

decisions.title: The shared tools now hold themselves to the same bar they hold your projects to
decisions.why: The forty-four breakages were run by nothing: they stood while somebody remembered to type the command, and the only automated caller was the racing project's push — the wrong repository, and it swallowed the answer. The shared tools now run them on their own commits, and only when the code the breakages are written against is what is changing. It caught something real on its first run: one breakage had quietly stopped being caught by anything.

decisions.title: Both guards read a command through one shared piece, not one each
decisions.why: They already shared the list of words that can be put in front of a command, and still drifted: one of them stripped those words' own switches and the other did not, so the same disguise that the line guard refused walked a commit past the card check. Sharing the list was not enough — the reading itself is now shared, and a disguise closed anywhere is closed everywhere.

next.if_nothing: The protection stays exactly as it is. The shared work project is shut to agents on both its shipping lines and your own three are unchanged; the job finishes itself once a reading comes back with nothing.

steps.step: A reading comes back with nothing to send back — sixteen in a row have found something
The copy this was built in is removed and the job closes
